script: A philosopher chose death over surrender—why? Jacques‑Louis David painted this dramatic scene in 1787, capturing Socrates’ final moments as he drinks hemlock before his Athenian judges. The canvas bursts with neoclassical clarity: marble statues loom, a bright sky, and a stoic Socrates surrounded by grieving students. David used oil on a massive 51‑by‑77‑inch canvas, layering thin glazes to give the figures a marble‑like sheen. Look closely at the young man in the foreground holding a lyre—he’s actually a symbol of the lost harmony of the Republic. Notice the broken column behind Socrates; it hints at the collapse of traditional values. Even the overturned cup of hemlock is rendered with a reflective glaze, emphasizing the poisonous choice. The painting’s composition forces your eye from the trembling pupils to Socrates’ calm hand, a visual lesson in stoic bravery. So, would you sip the poison if you stood in his place?
